transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hello, doctor. I’m here because I’m constantly forgetting little everyday things—appointments, errands, even finishing what I start for the community center. My husband and friends were actually worried I might be developing early dementia, but my primary care doctor suggested it might actually be a long-standing attention issue instead.

Have these attention and forgetfulness problems been present since childhood or your teen years, or did they start only later in adulthood? Were they fairly lifelong, or did they appear around the same time as any mood changes or a medical/neurologic illness?

They’ve actually been there my whole life; my childhood report cards always said I was bright but "daydreamed and talked out of turn," and I'd constantly wander off from my chores. I managed to compensate for decades with a strict work routine, but since retiring about two years ago, these lifelong struggles have really surfaced. It's not a sudden medical or mood change, just an old pattern that is much harder to manage now.
Do these attention problems still affect you in more than one part of your life, like at home, with friends, or when managing daily tasks? Can you give one or two examples of how they interfere?

Yes, they definitely affect me in multiple areas, both at home and with my volunteer work. At home, I'll completely miss a dentist appointment even though I keep a calendar on the fridge. At the community center, I've forgotten supply runs and mixed up dates so much that some volunteers have gently suggested I step back from leading projects.

Along with the inattention, have you also had lifelong problems with restlessness or impulsivity, like feeling driven to keep moving, talking excessively, interrupting others, or acting before thinking? If so, did those also start back in childhood?

Yes, I've always felt a constant need to keep moving, like I'm "on the go" and can't just sit still to relax, and I frequently find myself interrupting others or finishing their sentences during meetings. This definitely goes back to childhood; my school report cards often noted that I rushed and talked out of turn, and my mother constantly scolded me for wandering off from my chores.

Have there been long periods when your attention problems got much worse only during depression or during times you felt unusually energized, needed less sleep, and were more impulsive than usual? Or have these symptoms stayed fairly constant regardless of your mood?

No, these issues have been quite constant throughout my life and don't come and go with my mood. I've never experienced periods of depression or times where I felt unusually energized and didn't need sleep. Instead, they just became much more noticeable over the last two years because I lost my daily work routine when I retired.

final_diagnosis.reason: Lifelong pattern of inattention plus hyperactivity/impulsivity beginning in childhood, present across multiple settings, causing functional impairment, and not limited to mood episodes or a new medical/neurologic process. This is most consistent with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive subtype code available among the provided candidates.
